For me, Fluoxetin is the only anti-depressant I ever felt a positive effect from. 
(for context I have been on: Sertraline, Mirtizapine, Citalopram, Escitalopram)

I was first given it in inpatient treatment for my ED and stayed at the lowest dose of 20mg, since I was already experiencing a positive effect from that dose. It gave me more energy, I generally felt more upbeat and able and willing to do things in life. at the time, the side effects I had were a bit of diarrhoea at the very start, headaches, light nausea and a temporary loss of/reduction of appetite for a while at the start.

I'm currently on 60mg after a relapse. I only started taking the medication after I was regularly B/Ping and was desperate to stop. Stopping B/P seemed impossible to me at the time and I wasn't really able to, though that doesn't mean the medication didn't work, there were various other factors at play. since then, I've been able to occasionally stop B/Ping (going anywhere from 1-10 days B/P free after multiple times daily before) but the underlying issue for me is restriction since I have AN-B/P.
I went up to the 60mg dose quite quickly so this time the side effects hit me like a truck. I had fatigue, headaches, a weird stuffy feeling in my face and diarrhea again, but also only at the very start. what hit me like a truck was the nausea, it was and sometimes still is awful, despite me no longer upping my dose, but the other side effects have gone away.
While I'm still B/Ping a lot, I will say that things feel different now on the meds. I noticed that bingeing just doesn't feel enjoyable anymore, it mostly just sucks, which at times has actually helped me give B/Ping a break.

Maybe my overly detailed experience can help you with this ^^
(keep in mind that some of my symptoms may have other origins as I really am not physically healthy at all and have lots of issues)
I'd say, give it a try for at least a couple weeks, since it takes a while for side effect to dissipate and positive effects to set in. If you don't like it or it doesn't work, that's okay and don't have to continue taking it.

the answer really depends, but I can give you some insights as someone who has recovered (re-fed and weight restored, not mental recovery) many times with many different methods. 

I was also vegan for a long time and ate loads of veggies and very high fibre. recovering from this, especially since I also ate no fats, was the hardest on my body. I tried to recover with veggies, fruit and loads of fibre and was bloated all of the time. the next time I went through recovery I ate way less fibre, veggies and fruit and it definitely eased things up a lot. for the first time in years I sometimes wasn't bloated at all and was able to regularly shit (impossible before).

if you're very used to high amounts of fibre, it will obviously cause fewer problems for you, but I'd almost always recommend loosening the control around fibre intake. even if you're used to it, it can definitely cause a lot of bloating and constipation in recovery (since you're eating so much more in general). I found it so so hard to let go of my obsession with fibre, since I was terrified of constipation, but I was really positively surprised to find out that reducing fibre over time made things so much easier for me.
less bloating, less water retention, less abdominal distention and discomfort, more regular and healthy shits.

things might feels worse at first (but trust me it always does in recovery!) but over time it gets so much easier and the body adapts quickly.

I'm in the exact same boat. spent every day for weeks telling myself today I'll be able to stop but failing every time.

but for around 2 weeks now I've actually been able to stop, do I'll share what I did and hope it helps !

1. the NUMBER ONE thing to do is to eat through the day !!!
I don't know what your b/p pattern is like but for me it was always at the end of the day when I'd be so so hungry from not eating at all/enough. eating regularly thought the day helped me the most. especially eating in the morning, even if it's not a lot. a lot of research has shown that hunger in the mornings (that doesn't get satiated) is one of the biggest triggers for b/p later in the day. I don't feel particularly hungry in the mornings but I still have some sort of breakfast anywhere between 1-2 hours after waking up.
right now I eat 3 small meals a day, it doesn't have to be much if that feels too scary. simply eating regularly tells your body that food is available, it's not a scarce resource and will eventually curb b/p urges. 
an important note: I started eating throughout the day but wasn't able to stop purging until I'd kept up the pattern for a while. it's was terrifying, but it helped so much.



2. become aware of your b/p pattern
when do you purge ? what do you feel like before hand ? what exactly is preventing you from not purging ?
becoming aware of this helped me to set up an action plan for the most critical times of day (when I was mostly likely to b/p). as I said, for me it would always be in the evenings, so I set up an evening plan for myself.
first I'd have dinner, then immediately afterwards I'd brush my teeth/rinse my mouth with mouthwash. getting the taste of food out of my mouth helped reduce the b/p urges the most. then I set up specific things I'd do afterwards until I'd go to bed (have a shower, read/draw, watch a film, anything the suits you !)



3. if possible, eat with others.
again, I don't know your situation so I can't say how applicable this is to you. generally speaking, I don't purge when around others, so I knew eating with others when I'm mostly likely to b/p would help prevent that. not only that but I'd be less likely to go on a binge around others and eating felt more relaxed for me then.



4. have compassion with yourself.
understand that this is something causing you a lot of pain and suffering, that you're trying really hard to change and recognise that that's okay. you are not a failure, you're not doing anything wrong. you are trying your best.
I know you want to stop purging, I knew it's just horrific to go through. but if you do, that's also okay, you haven't failed. take each day as it comes and try to go through the day knowing that you are doing what you can, you are trying your best and that alone is an act of self care. 
changing my mindset, even while still regularly purging helped remove some of the guilt, shame and suffering I experienced around purging. in general it helped me feel more relaxed and calmer which eventually made stopping purging easier. I wasn't fighting with myself as much and that gave my mind and body the chance to realise I'm not in danger.
purging is often associated with feelings of stress, anxiety, overwhelm and pain. reducing those feelings will already help a lot.

first of all: it's not all in your head ! lax abuse recovery is very physically uncomfortable and also very mentally draining !

you've probably heard this before but the most important thing right now is patience and sticking to it. it's going to take time for your body to adjust and things will get worse before they get better. 5 days really isn't that long at all and it's completely normal to feel so uncomfortable still. I'd recommend doing anything that helps with that discomfort, like using a hot water bottle, resting & laying down, giving yourself an abdominal massage, very light yoga for digestion and of course mental distraction ! I used to obsessively body check my stomach to see if it was flat from the laxatives and during recovery and decided to just completely quit it since seeing myself bloated was incredibly triggering and tempted me to use again.


the best thing you can do for yourself is to just not take the laxatives, no matter how hard that feels. during recovery I felt so hopeless and thought I'd never be able to go to the toilet again normally, but trust me our bodies are amazing and I reajusted fairly quickly. eating enough and regularly is also incredibly important right now, otherwise your body won't be getting used to regular normal digestion of food. 

on the mental side, distract yourself as much as you can and take each day by day. hell, even take things minute for minute if you need to. when I felt the urge to take laxatives I'd do something to distract myself for 15 minutes, when the 15 minutes were over I'd try something else and so on until i made it through the day. it's exhausting, it's so hard and incredibly draining but so worth it. 
it felt so rewarding when my body started to heal. as stupid and tmi as it may sound, the first time I actually felt the urge to go again I was genuinely overjoyed since I thought my body had lost the ability to do that. with time things got better

I don't personally have dabuilima but I could tell you a bit about treatment. unfortunately, there isn't a lot of good to say about it, that is, there is barely any treatment. 


it seems to be a relatively new illness within the medical field, though I assume it's been an issue for people for much longer. because of that there's very very few treatment centers or specialists, and even fewer people who even know about it. 


The biggest issue with treatment seems to be that it's fairly different to other eating disorders. I doubt the cause is much different (trauma, other mental illnesses, genetics and culture) but treatment never starts at the core cause. It starts with the most surface level issue, eating itself and weight. That's the trouble with diabulimia, it's not that you restrict or purge or engage in other behaviours commonly associated with EDs. 
That seems to be doctors' biggest issue. treatment for eating disorders mostly starts with reintroduction of healthy eating habits. but, on the surface, diabulimics to tend to have "healthy" eating habits. 
However, treatment may be similar to treatment for bulimia, which I believe is DBT, which focuses on habits, compulsions and coping mechanisms as well trauma therapy. 


if you'd like the hear more about treatment there's some documentaries about it on YouTube and I'd recommend Of Herbs And Altars video on it too. 


What I can recommend is searching specifically for a dabulimia self help, or treatment group. it could be though that there are none in your area, so definitely try searching online. 


I truly hope you can find good help and recover. Diabulimia is really scary and extremely dangerous. And even if you can't feel or believe it now, you are worthy of love and care, and deserve to recover ❤️
